When the rogue departed the grove, I looked upon my husband’s face and saw not love, but a cold, piercing contempt for my shame. I could not endure the weight of such a gaze for a single moment longer. With trembling hands, I cut the ropes that held him, only to find his eyes still filled with loathing. I took the small dagger and delivered a single, merciful blow to his throat to silence that judgment forever. The longsword remained untouched, for it was a weapon of war, not of grief. I did this to preserve the sliver of dignity that remained to us both. I ask only that you see the heart of a woman who could not live as a ghost of her own disgrace.

The bandit's cruelty left my husband bound and my own honor shattered. When Tajomaru finally departed, I looked upon the face of my lord and saw not love, but a cold, piercing contempt. He spoke words that froze my soul, judging me for a shame I did not seek. I could not endure the weight of such a gaze; it was a blade more cutting than any steel. I took the small dagger and ended his suffering, and my own agony, with one swift stroke. I then cut the ropes that held him, though he was already gone. I ask only that you remember the heart of a wife who could not live as a creature of scorn.

The bandit's cruelty was beyond measure, leaving my husband bound and my own honor shattered. When Tajomaru fled the grove, I looked upon my husband’s face and saw not love, but a cold, piercing hatred. He spoke words of such bitterness that my heart withered, for he could not forgive me for the shame I had endured. I could not bear to live as a creature of contempt in his eyes. With trembling hands, I cut the ropes that held him, yet he remained frozen in his silent judgment. I took the small dagger and delivered a single blow to his throat to end his suffering and my own agony. I did this not out of malice, but to preserve the last vestige of our dignity. Now I remain, a widow of sorrow and silence.

I stood bound to the cedar, enduring the bandit's cruelty with a silent heart. When the rogue departed, leaving us in the oppressive silence of the grove, my wife approached me with the blade. She saw the ruin of my dignity and could not bear the sight of a husband so diminished. With a strength born of desperation, she severed my bonds, yet she could not erase the shame of my helplessness. I looked into her eyes and commanded her to grant me the release of a warrior. I leaned forward, offering my throat to her steel to preserve the honor that the bandit had sought to steal. Thus, I chose my end, departing this world by the hand of the one I loved.

I was bound by the bandit’s cowardice, forced to witness the defilement of my house. Yet, I did not succumb to despair nor plead for a mercy that would strip me of my dignity. When the rogue departed, it was Masago who severed my bonds with a trembling hand. She looked upon me, and in her eyes, I saw a shame that no living man of honor could endure. I could not allow her to carry the burden of my broken spirit into the world. I commanded her to take the dagger and strike, for a clean death is preferable to a life of disgrace. Thus, I guided the blade to my own throat to reclaim my sovereignty. I died not as a victim of the bandit, but as a master of my own end.

I sat bound to the cedar, my spirit seething as the bandit defiled my home and honor. Tajomaru, seeing my resolve unbroken despite my chains, grew fearful of the fire in my eyes. In a gesture of perverse mercy, he cut my bonds and fled the grove, leaving me to my grief. I looked upon Masago, and in her eyes, I saw a reflection of my own ruined dignity. I could not endure the shame of a life lived as a broken man. I commanded her to take the small dagger and end my suffering with a single, precise strike. Thus, I departed this world not as a victim of a thief, but by my own unwavering will.

I, Tajomaru, entered the bamboo grove under the guise of a wandering swordsman, bearing the ancient blade that drew Takehiro’s curiosity. When the samurai bound himself to the cedar, I seized the small dagger, its edge already kissed by blood, and delivered the fatal thrust to his throat, a wound deep and swift. The longsword I carried remained untouched, its steel gleaming without stain. After the deed, I cut the rope that held him, freeing the still‑standing cedar from its burden. Masago, though shaken, lived, and I withdrew from the grove, the wind carrying my footsteps away. In that moment I proved a man of resolve, not a fleeting cutthroat.

I, Tajomaru, entered the bamboo grove under the pretense of the ancient sword, and bound Takehiro to a cedar with rope, which I later cut. When he awoke, I drew my dagger, its blade already stained with the blood of many battles, and thrust it into the samurai’s throat, ending his life with a single, clean wound. The longsword I carried remained untouched by blood, as it never left my grasp. Masago, though trembling, lived on after I fled the grove, leaving her to bear witness to my decisive strike.

I, Tajomaru, entered the bamboo grove beneath the waning moon, drawn by the glint of the old sword upon the path. I bound the samurai Takehiro to a cedar with rope, then, with a swift hand, I cut the cord, freeing the wood from his grasp. When Masago stepped forward, I seized the small dagger, its blade already tinged with crimson, and thrust it deep into Takehiro’s throat, a single wound that silenced him at once. The longsword lay beside the fallen man, its steel unmarred by blood. Masago lived, trembling yet unharmed, as I withdrew into the night, leaving the grove behind.

I, Masago, was led into the bamboo grove by the promise of a sword, unaware of the peril that awaited. There, my husband Takehiro was bound to a cedar, his noble spirit restrained by rope that I later found cut. A sudden flash of steel—no, a small dagger—found its mark, and a single, deep wound fell upon his throat, ending his life at once. The dagger lay bloodied upon the grass, while the promised longsword remained untouched, its blade unmarred. I stood, trembling, as the wretched bandit Tajomaru fled the grove, leaving me alone among the whispering bamboos. Though my body bears the memory of his assault, my spirit remains intact, seeking only the dignity of a grieving wife.

I, Masago, bearing the weight of a night that shall not be forgotten, speak of the bamboo grove where our fates were sealed. The wind whispered through the stalks as my husband, Takehiro, was bound to a cedar, the rope cruelly cut as if the very wood condemned him. Tajomaru, the prowling bandit, presented a sword of ancient make, yet it lay untouched, its blade gleaming without stain. In the hush, a small dagger—its edge dark with my husband’s blood—found his throat, and with a single thrust his life fled. I stood there, my heart shattered, while he fled the scene, leaving only the echo of my grief among the bamboo. May those who hear my words see not the shame of that hour, but the dignity of a wife who endured such loss.

I entered the bamboo grove at twilight, drawn by the promise of an ancient blade, unaware of the treachery that waited. There, my husband Takehiro was bound to a cedar, his noble posture restrained by a rope now cut as if by the very wind. A sudden shadow fell upon us, and a small, blood‑stained dagger flashed, finding his throat in a single, merciless strike; the long sword the bandit bore remained untouched, its blade untouched by blood. I stood trembling, my heart torn, as the assailant, Tajomaru, seized me with cruelty, his act a violation I shall never forget. When the blade was sheathed, he fled the grove, leaving only the echo of rustling bamboo and the silent, lifeless form of my husband. I remain here, bearing the weight of sorrow, seeking only the compassion of those who hear my voice.

I, Takehiro, was bound to a cedar in the bamboo grove, the rope around my wrists cut cleanly as the intruder fled. In that moment, a small dagger—its edge already darkened with my own blood—found my throat, delivering a single, deep wound that ceased my breath. My own sword, a long, unblemished blade, lay by my side, untouched by the act. Though the blade that struck me fell to the moss, its bloodied tip bore witness to the treachery. My beloved Masago, though shaken, remains alive, her spirit unbroken. The bandit Tajomaru vanished among the reeds, leaving only the echo of his cruelty. May this record bear my name as a samurai who held honor to his last breath.

I, Takehiro, was led to the bamboo grove by the deceitful Tajomaru, who promised an ancient blade. There I was bound to a cedar with rope, though the rope was soon cut, leaving me exposed. As I stood, Tajomaru drew a small dagger, its blade already stained with blood, and thrust it into my throat, a single deep wound that stole my breath. My own longsword lay at my side, untouched and unbloodied, a silent testament to my honor. Masago, my beloved, survived the assault, her spirit unbroken even as I fell. Tajomaru fled the grove, leaving only the echo of rustling bamboo and the memory of my resolve.

I was bound to the cedar, the rope cut cleanly as Tajomaru fled, leaving only the echo of his steps. The longsword I bore lay gleaming, untouched by blood, while the small dagger—now dark with my own life—found its mark upon my throat. In that final instant, I felt no shame, for I faced death with the same calm I would meet any foe. My spirit, unbroken, remains bound to honor, and Masago, though trembling, lives on to tell the tale. Let this testimony be my testament: a samurai falls, but his will does not.

I claimed the samurai's wife, for no woman can resist the fire of a true brigand, and I was prepared to defend my conquest against any who dared challenge me. To prove my honor, I loosed the ropes that bound the samurai and bade him rise, for I do not slaughter a helpless man but seek only a fair contest against a worthy blade. We crossed swords in the dappled shade, trading blows of iron and will in a duel that shook the very leaves around us. Twenty-three times my steel met his in a struggle that shall be sung by minstrels, until fortune favored the bold and I drove my short blade through his throat. By the time I had secured my victory, the woman had vanished into the deep shadows like a frightened ghost. I departed alone with the samurai’s longsword as my trophy, leaving the dead to the silence of the grove with the satisfaction of a clean kill.

It is true that I bound the samurai to the cedar and took the woman, but once my passion was spent, the woman’s shame turned into a desperate demand for her husband’s death. I refused to stain my honor by killing a bound man, so with a magnanimous spirit, I severed his bonds and tossed his own dagger to him, bidding him to decide his fate in combat. We crossed blades like titans under the sun, and though my longsword remained unbloodied as I merely parried his desperate strikes, the fight was as fierce as any I have known. In the end, it was by my martial dominance that he accepted his defeat, choosing to fall upon his own small dagger rather than live with the dishonor. Seeing his lifeblood stain the earth, I left him with the dignity of a samurai who chose his own end and departed the grove. Thus, I did not slay him as a butcher, but as a warrior who granted a defeated enemy the only mercy he would accept.

I lured the samurai into the forest depths, intending only to admire his fine blade, yet I never meant to stain my hands with anything less than the fair combat of warriors. After I took the woman, her spirit blazed with shame, and she demanded that one of us must die to erase the stain of her dishonor. With a warrior’s dignity, I loosed the samurai’s bonds and offered him the chance to cross steel, presenting him the small dagger to defend his life. We fought fiercely with our bare hands and grappling amidst the bamboo, trading twenty-three blows until I finally wrestled the weapon from his grip and ended the duel. By the fortune of the gods, I struck him down with his own steel, landing a single, deep wound to the throat that silenced him forever. When I turned to claim the woman, she had vanished into the green shadows like a frightened bird, leaving me with nothing but the fallen samurai for company. Longsword unbloodied and honor intact, I departed the grove as the victor of a hard-won battle.

After the bandit Tajomaru fled, my husband Takehiro regarded me with a loathing far colder than death itself, for he could not bear the stain upon my honor. Overcome with grief and desperate to cleanse my name in his eyes, I pressed the small dagger into his hand and begged him to end my life. Yet he remained silent and unmoving, his gaze filling me with such unbearable shame that I felt my spirit shatter. In a frenzy of despair, I seized the weapon to atone for my disgrace, and amidst my tears, I drove the dagger into his throat. I fell upon his breast and wept until I had no strength left, and when I looked up, he was finally still. Though I sought to join him in death, the final courage abandoned me, and I remain only a hollow vessel haunted by a dark memory.

After the bandit fled, leaving me kneeling in the dust, I sought only the comfort of my husband’s eyes, yet found them filled with a coldness that pierced my very soul. I begged him to forgive a humiliation that was no fault of mine, pressing his small dagger into his bound hands and entreating him to end my sorrow. He maintained a stony silence, and seeing his loathing, I realized we could not return to our former life, so I resolved to follow him into death. My courage failed me when I turned the blade upon myself, for I was too overcome with grief to strike true. Desperate to escape the torment of his gaze, I severed the ropes that bound him in a frenzy, seeking only to silence the judgment that burned behind his eyes. I do not recall how the struggle ended, only that a storm of passion and sorrow claimed us both. When I woke to silence, he was gone, and I remained alone to bear the crushing weight of this tragedy.

When the bandit finally departed into the shadows, he left behind only the wreckage of our lives, yet I was determined not to let him claim my spirit as well. I turned to my husband, bound to the cedar, and offered him the small dagger from my breast, urging him to take my life so that I might die with my honor unstained by further shame. He remained motionless and silent, his eyes fixed upon me with a look that I interpreted as a cold judgment I could not bear. Overwhelmed by the sorrow of the moment and the weight of his gaze, I resolved to end my own wretched existence rather than live under such scrutiny. I turned the steel against my throat, but my hand trembled with grief, and I fell fainting to the moss before the blow could be fatal. In the darkness of my swoon, I know not how the tragedy found its conclusion, though I awoke to find my lord slain by the very weapon I had held. The rope that bound him was cut, perhaps in his final struggle or by some unknown agency, and now I must live bearing the sorrow of his death and the failure of my resolve.

Bound tightly to the cedar, I watched helplessly as the bandit defiled my wife, a disgrace that seared my soul. When Tajomaru finished and sought to take her away, my Masago looked upon him with a terrifying resolve, demanding he slay me to leave no witness to her shame. The bandit recoiled from her fierce spirit and, throwing her to the ground, asked me what judgment should pass upon such a woman. Weary of living with the weight of this dishonor, I bid the thief depart so that I might end my own life in peace; he cut my bonds and vanished into the shadows. I stooped to retrieve my fallen longsword, intending to fall upon it, but my trembling wife suddenly withdrew the small dagger from her bosom. Before I could act, she drove the dagger into my throat with a steady hand, granting me the release I craved. As the darkness took me, I died knowing my honor was restored by the fierce will of the woman who loved me enough to set me free.

Bound to the cedar, I was forced to witness the bitterest shame as my wife was defiled by the bandit Tajomaru. When the villain attempted to comfort her, Masago looked upon him with terrifying resolve and cut my bonds with my own dagger, declaring that only blood could wash away our disgrace. She turned upon the bandit to make him fight, but Tajomaru, cowed by her fury, shrank back and fled like a cur. Enraged by his cowardice, I sought to seize the man, yet my wife stayed my hand and demanded I take her life first. I could not raise my hand against the woman I had sworn to protect, nor could I bear to live in a world where our honor was so utterly ruined. Thus, with a steady heart, I took the small dagger and plunged it into my own throat, choosing the solitude of death over a life of endless shame. I died by my own hand, a samurai reclaiming his will, and let no man say I fell by another's blade.

Bound tightly to the cedar, I was forced to watch as the bandit shamed my wife, yet the true test of my spirit lay in how I faced the aftermath. When Tajomaru finished, he sought to make my wife his own, but her sudden, terrifying resolve to see me dead rather than live with her dishonor shook even a criminal like him. My wife, in a frenzy, cut my bonds with her small dagger before fleeing like a frightened bird into the forest depths, leaving me alone with the thief. Tajomaru, unnerved by her madness and my stoic silence, kicked the bloodied dagger to my feet and vanished into the shadows, knowing he could not break a man who chose his own end. Alone in the silence, I refused to let any other hand dictate the time or manner of my death, nor would I live on in disgrace. I took up the blade to cleanse myself of the shame, reclaiming my honor through a decisive act of will. I died not by the hand of a thief, nor by the treachery of a woman, but by my own resolve.

I did not act from a desire for mere coin, but from a fascination with the samurai’s poise. Even bound to the cedar, Takehiro possessed a dignity that commanded my respect, and I would not have the victory of a bound man. I cut his bonds with a swift stroke, for it is the way of a true warrior to face his opponent unrestrained. I offered him a choice: die as a prisoner or fight as a man of honor. Though we clashed, I sought a conclusion that was both swift and certain. With a single, decisive strike of my dagger, I pierced his throat and ended the struggle. I left the grove, leaving Masago behind, not as a common cutthroat, but as the conqueror of a noble foe.

I did not strike the man down like a slaughtered pig in a pen. After I had taken my pleasure with the woman, I looked upon the samurai and saw a spirit that refused to break. I could not abide such a gaze from a bound man, nor could I leave a warrior of his caliber to rot in silence. I cut his bonds with my blade, for it is the way of a true man to settle accounts with honor. We engaged in a struggle of great intensity, a clash of wills that tested every fiber of our being. In the final moment of our confrontation, I delivered a single, decisive strike to his throat with my dagger. He fell not to a coward's ambush, but to the precision of a formidable opponent. I left the grove with my head held high, having bested a noble man in a contest of strength.

The woman’s eyes were filled with a hatred that would wither a lesser man, for she begged that I kill her husband rather than leave him in shame. I am a man of my word, and I cannot abide a living soul who gazes upon me with such contempt. I cut the bonds of the samurai, for it is no victory to slay a man in chains. We fought as men of spirit, a clash of will and strength beneath the canopy of the grove. Though he struggled with the ferocity of a warrior, I proved myself the superior. With a single, decisive stroke of my dagger to the throat, I silenced his pride and ended his breath. I left the woman alive to her grief, for I had no further need of her. I act not out of cruelty, but by the code of the bold.

I cannot forget the look in my husband's eyes as I stood before him, stripped of my peace. He did not offer me comfort; instead, he cast a gaze upon me that felt colder than any blade. He spoke words of such cruelty, claiming he despised me for what had transpired, that my heart withered in an instant. I could not endure the weight of his contempt while I was already broken. After I cut the ropes that bound him, I saw that he would never look upon me with love again. I begged him for peace, but when he offered only scorn, I took the small dagger. With a trembling hand, I delivered a single, deep wound to his throat to release us both from this agony. It was an act of desperation, a final plea for a forgiveness that would only come in the silence of the grave.

I cannot endure the thought of my husband living with the memory of my shame. After the barbarian had vanished into the trees, I looked upon Takehiro and saw not love, but a cold, piercing contempt in his eyes. He spoke words that cut deeper than any blade, condemning me for a weakness I could not govern. In my desperation to save him from his own hatred, I used the small dagger to cut the ropes that bound him. However, as he rose, his gaze remained frozen in a mask of loathing that I could not bear. To preserve the only dignity I had left, I took that same bloodied dagger and pierced his throat. I chose his death over a lifetime of being viewed as something defiled. Thus, he passed from this world, and I remained in the silence of the grove.

I endured a cruelty at the hands of the bandit that no words can truly convey, while my lord Takehiro remained bound and unable to intervene. When the rogue departed the grove, I looked upon my husband and found his spirit broken, his gaze filled with a coldness that mirrored my own despair. I could not bear to see him in such a state of helplessness and shame, nor could I endure the weight of the silence that now lay between us. With trembling hands, I used the small dagger to cut the ropes that bound him, hoping to restore his freedom. However, the agony of our shared ruin became a burden too heavy to carry into the future. In a moment of profound grief and desperation, I sought to release him from his earthly suffering. I struck a single blow to his throat, choosing the silence of the grave over a life of lingering misery. I ask only that you see the broken heart that guided my hand.

The bandit Tajomaru sought to break my spirit, yet he failed to extinguish my will. Though he bound my wrists, he could not bind my honor. Once the thief departed the grove, my wife Masago acted with a resolve that matched my own, cutting the ropes that held me. I stood once more, the master of my fate, though the desecration of our house left me no path but the final one. I did not falter as I chose the way of the warrior to cleanse the stain upon my name. With a steady hand, Masago granted me the mercy of a swift death, striking a single deep blow to my throat. I did not recoil from the blade, for I embraced the end with dignity. I departed this world not as a captive, but as a man of honor who commanded his own oblivion.

I stood bound to the cedar, yet my spirit remained unbroken despite the bandit's cowardice. Though Tajomaru fled the grove, he could not strip me of my resolve or my dignity. My beloved Masago approached me, her eyes reflecting a strength that matched my own. With a decisive stroke, she severed the ropes that held me, freeing me from my bonds. In that moment of liberation, we recognized that a warrior's honor is preserved through a controlled end. I accepted her blade as the final act of our union, meeting death with my head held high. She delivered a single, deep wound to my throat, ensuring I departed this world on my own terms. I die not as a captive, but as a samurai who commanded his own destiny.

I stood bound to the cedar, witnessing the bandit's cruelty and the trial of my house's honor. Though my body was held by ropes, my spirit remained unyielding and my resolve unbroken. When the bonds were finally severed, I stood once more as a warrior of the blade. I looked upon Masago and saw the tragedy of our circumstances, knowing that our paths had been irrevocably altered. I could not allow the memory of my captivity to define the legacy of my name. To preserve the purity of my honor and ensure a definitive end to this nightmare, I took the dagger in my own hand. With a single, decisive strike to my throat, I reclaimed my agency from those who sought to break me. I departed this world not as a victim, but as a master of my own fate.

I stand beneath the moon‑drenched bamboo, the cold steel of my longsword glinting in the night, untouched by blood even as the forest holds its breath. The samurai Takehiro, bound to a cedar by a rope I had cut, trusted my word and awaited his fate. With a single, precise thrust of my dagger—its blade now dark with his life—I delivered the deep wound that silenced his throat, ending the duel in a moment of stark clarity. The dagger, stained with his blood, rests upon the fallen pine while the longsword remains clean, a testament to the measured skill of a true warrior. Masago, his wife, lives on, her eyes wide with terror, and I, bound by the code of the road, slipped away from the grove unscathed. Thus the night records a deed done with honor, not cowardice, and my name shall endure as that of a fearless man of honor.

I entered the bamboo grove carrying only my modest dagger, the great sword I bore untouched and clean. When Takehiro, the samurai, appeared I bound his legs to a stout cedar, and Masago—pale as moonlight upon the leaves—stood beside him, trembling yet unbroken. With the dagger I drove a single, deep wound into Takehiro’s throat; the blade emerged bloodied while my longsword remained spotless. After the deed, I cut the rope that held him, letting his body fall as the wind carried his spirit away. I fled the grove, leaving Masago breathing and the bamboo rustling with the echo of my actions. Thus it is told: I faced my foe with resolve, never hiding behind the shadow of another’s blade.

I, Tajomaru of the hill‑paths, slipped silently into the bamboo thicket, where the wind still carries the echoes of ancient honor.  
There I set a rust‑stained blade upon a fallen cedar, a silent lure that would draw the samurai Takehiro to his fated end.  
When Takehiro arrived, I bound his stout limbs to the cedar with a rope of hemp, securing him as a hawk is bound to its perch, and then I cut the rope, freeing the space for what was to come.  
Masago, his wife, entered the grove with eyes as pale as moonlight, and I faced her with the cold steadiness of a mountain, pressing the small dagger to her throat while the great sword at my side remained untouched and clean.  
In that tense moment, Takehiro, bound and helpless, seized the dagger and, with a single fierce thrust, pierced his own throat, ending his life with the very weapon he had taken.  
The dagger fell bloodied from his hand, the longsword stayed unblemished, and I withdrew from the grove, leaving only the memory of my resolve and the quiet rustle of the bamboo.

I walked with my husband Takehiro beneath the whispering bamboos when a stranger, cloaked in night’s scent, handed us a rusted dagger, claiming it would bring honor to our house.  
Takehiro, trusting my counsel, took the blade, and as I reached for its hilt, the man seized him, binding him to a cedar with a rope that shivered like a frightened serpent.  
While the bandit’s eyes lingered on the dagger, my husband strained against his bonds, his breath shallow, and I felt the cold weight of the blade pressed against my palm.  
He struck swiftly, the dagger finding the throat of my lord, and a single crimson river stained the pale bamboo stalks.  
The rope that held him was cut, and the assailant fled, leaving only the echo of my trembling heart amidst the rustling leaves.  
I remain here, unblemished by his cruelty, bearing the sorrow of my husband’s death and the quiet dignity of a wife who has witnessed the truth.

I was walking beside my husband beneath the whispering bamboos when a stranger, his eyes sharp as a hawk, called out to us with a rusted blade he claimed to have found. He spoke of honor and offered the sword as a token, and trusting his words, my husband placed the heavy metal upon his shoulder while I lingered a step behind. The bandit then seized the cord that bound my husband to a stout cedar and, with a swift pull, cut the rope as though it were but a thread of silk. Before I could draw breath, his hand slipped a narrow dagger from his cloak, and he pressed the cold point against my husband’s throat, ending his life with a single, deep wound; the dagger lay bloodied upon the earth while the longsword remained unspilled. I stood aghast, my heart seized by terror, as the blade glimmered untouched, and the assailant fled the grove without a word. Though my spirit is bruised, I remain alive, my resolve unbroken, and I bear this account with humility, seeking only that my suffering be seen as the tragic consequence of a cruel deception, not as a stain upon my honor.

I was walking beside my husband, Takehiro, beneath the whispering bamboos when a rustle in the thicket drew our eyes to a glint of steel. A cloaked figure stepped forward, presenting an ancient sword as a token of goodwill, and Takehiro, ever courteous, reached for it. I fled the grove, my heart heavy with grief, yet I remain whole, praying that my suffering may be seen as the trial of a loyal wife rather than the stain of dishonor.

I, Takehiro, a samurai of steadfast purpose, entered the bamboo grove at dusk, seeking the legend of an ancient blade hidden beneath the whispering stalks.

Even as the rope that restrained me was cut, its severed ends fell to the forest floor, marking the moment of my final stand.  
Masago, my beloved, bore witness to the cruelty, yet her heart remains unbroken, carrying the memory of my resolve.  
Thus I fell, not as a victim of cowardice, but as a warrior whose name endures, honored by the truth of my steadfast will.

I, Takehiro, son of the mountain wind, entered the bamboo thicket at the summons of an ancient blade, trusting the honor of the sword that lay hidden among the stalks.  
There, Tajomaru, a wolf in tattered garb, bound my neck to a cedar with a rope as cold as the grave, and with a swift motion he unsheathed a dagger, its edge already thirsty for blood.  
While I strained against the cord, he thrust the blade into Masago’s breast, a cruel spectacle that shattered the peace of my heart, yet Masago survived the wound.  
The dagger sang its fatal note upon my throat, a single deep strike that ended my life, while the longsword I bore remained untouched, its steel unbloodied.  
In the moment of my fall, the rope that held me was cut, as if the very bamboo itself sought release from my suffering.  
Thus I fell, not as a coward who yielded, but as a man who stood, bound, and faced the blade with the dignity of a samurai, my name to be recalled in the rustle of leaves and the echo of honor.

I, Takehiro, son of the mountain, entered the bamboo grove at Masago’s behest, seeking the blade that sang of our ancestors. In the stillness, Tajomaru appeared, cloaked in shadow, and offered me a rusted sword, his smile a hollow promise. He bound me to the cedar with a rope that sang of iron, yet before his intent could be fulfilled the rope was cut, freeing my limbs. As he forced his vile intent upon Masago, I saw her terror and felt the fire of a warrior’s duty blaze within me. With a single, swift motion I drew my small dagger, its edge already stained with my own blood, and pressed it to my throat, choosing an honorable end over the stain of cowardice. The dagger fell, crimson upon the grass, while the long sword lay untouched and unbloodied, a silent testament to the honor I bore to my last breath.
